kurz: Parboil potatoes briefly in slightly alkaline water and shake them in the pot. The rough, starchy surface turns into a thick crust in the oven.
bild_im_kopf: Like sandpaper instead of glass: a rough surface has many more spots that can turn crisp.
was_passiert: The baking soda makes the water slightly alkaline. That loosens the glue between the outer cells faster; the edge turns soft while the core stays firm. When shaken, the edge rubs into a starchy mash that coats every piece. In the hot oven this mash dries into a crisp, craggy crust.
warum_wichtig: This is the opposite of soaking and still works. Both routes control starch and water on the surface, just with a different goal: a thin, smooth crust or a thick, craggy one.
faustregeln: Let them steam dry: wet potatoes do not roast.
Better too little baking soda than too much, or it turns soapy and mushy.
typische_fehler: Parboiled too long: the pieces fall apart completely when shaken.
schritte: Cut the potatoes into large pieces and start them in cold, well-salted water.
Add about ½ tsp baking soda per 2 litres of water.
Simmer until a knife slides easily into the edge but the core still resists.
Drain and let them steam dry for 1–2 minutes.
Shake hard in the pot with hot fat until the edges are rough and mushy.
Spread out on the preheated tray and roast at 220 °C, turning once.
